summary.title: Test smarter, not harder
summary.one_liner: Learn to cut unnecessary automated tests by weighing their value against their cost, writing tests against the API you wish existed, and pushing loops into the test so the computer does the repetitive work.
takeaways: Only write a test when its estimated value (regression catching, refactoring confidence, documentation) exceeds its estimated cost (writing, run time, maintenance, false failures).
Write test code against the helper API you wish existed, then implement that API, rather than copying verbose low-level driver code.
Use other correctness methods such as code review, static typing, introspection and property-based testing instead of tests where they are more effective.
Push loops inside a single test (e.g. check all entry points for authentication) so the computer runs the iteration instead of the developer writing many tests.
Seek help and existing tools rather than struggling alone; painful test writing is often a sign something is wrong.
summary.summary: The author argues that automated tests should be written selectively, not in large quantities out of a sense of duty. He frames the approach as a cost-benefit judgement: tests add run time, maintenance and false failures, and should be kept only when they catch regressions or enable refactoring. The article offers concrete techniques, including writing tests against an idealised helper API, relying on static typing, code review, introspection and hypothesis for property testing, and "pushing the loop in" so one test checks every entry point. It criticises a rote, painful approach to testing (and TDD followed as a ritual) and rejects Uncle Bob's advice to write lots of tests.
